newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan war moves closer to Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Afghan war moves closer to Kabul.

text.p: Refugees packed up all they had on their donkeys on Sunday as the forces of the ousted Afghan government and the Taleban militia battled for control of a village just north of Kabul.
The sound of battle was all around Kalakan, 30 km (20 miles) north of Kabul on Sunday morning.

Taleban fighters poured mortar and artillery fire and rockets at positions around the village. The sound of heavy small arms fire appeared to be coming from it, but it was not clear who was in control.

Villagers in the area said the forces of ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood had also surrounded a Taleban force between the Bagram air base, 60 km (40 miles) from Kabul, and the market town of Qarabagh on the main road north.

Masood's men, backed by the artillery of northern Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum, took Bagram and Qarabagh on Saturday and pushed another five km (three miles) down the road to Kabul to attack Kalakan later in the day, witnesses said.
Masood spokesman Mirabuddin Astana told reporters north of the front line that troops of the former government were just six km (four miles) from the outskirts of Kabul on the main road north.
He said they were 30 km (18 miles) from the city on the so-called new road which leads from Kabul to Bagram, then swings west to join the main road.
But reporters who travelled close to the front line from Kabul on Sunday morning saw no evidence of Masood's troops closer to the capital than Kalakan.
Villagers just behind the front lines said they had not seen or heard of any Masood soldiers in the area, and some said they would welcome such a presence.

"We are absolutely fed up of the Taleban. If Masood would give us some help, we would fight them," said one grey-bearded old man who said his family was getting ready to leave as the war inched closer to their farm.
He alleged that on Friday, the Moslem day of rest, the Taleban had summoned people in the area to the mosque, where they said an announcement would be made.
"They locked the doors and started beating people. Some they took away and locked them up in a container. When our mullah (Islamic priest) went to ask why, they beat him too," the old man said.
The people were released in the afternoon after several hours' detention resulting from a Taleban belief that they were Masood supporters, he said.
"They also come and make us cook food for them. We're really angry," he added.

Scores of people had already given up hope of holding on to their homes. A steady stream of people driving heavily laden donkeys walked towards Kabul down a road deserted except for Taleban vehicles, including two tanks, heading for the front.
The official news agency Bakhtar said more Taleban reinforcements were arriving in Kabul. It said 500 fighters had arrived from Paktia province south of the capital.
The Taleban, who took Kabul three weeks ago and imposed Islam's stern Sharia law on the capital, have rejected a Masood demand they quit the city to spare it another bloodbath.
The militia has enough men to defend the city, they said, but that might be difficult if Dostum joins the battle.
He sent tanks, artillery and men to join Masood on the front line last week, but Taleban fighters say they have seen no evidence so far that they have taken an active part.
Afghan watchers said Dostum appeared to be keeping his options open as he negotiated with the Taleban. The two sides have held a series of talks over the past few days, with no apparent result.
"They still appear to be far apart and the suspicion is that if Dostum does commit his forces, the talks will end," said one.
